rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. Moderate temperature and gradient duration provide a useful baseline for identifying critical pairs before refining slope and selectivity.

Double the gradient duration while holding composition endpoints and temperature fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. All eight peaks eluted early in the first run, so this shallower diagnostic gradient should retain ample acquisition margin.
Keep the shallower gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity at the remaining close pair. Higher temperature should also reduce the small time penalty from injection 2.
An intermediate temperature may avoid the co-elution at 60 C while preserving the improved separation of the earlier cluster. Slightly shortening the gradient targets a last peak below 10 minutes.

Lengthen the gradient one step at 55 C to improve the remaining critical pair while retaining the favorable temperature selectivity. The last peak should remain close to 10 minutes, limiting any time penalty.

The critical early pair responds weakly to duration at 55 C but separated well at 60 C. Use 60 C with a substantially steeper gradient to test whether the later co-elution can be broken while keeping the run comfortably below 10 minutes.

Injection 6 is nearly fully resolved; slightly narrow the gradient window to improve the early critical pair while shifting selectivity through a higher starting organic fraction. The substantial time margin allows this adjustment without risking a time penalty.

Slightly reduce the endpoint from injection 7 to spread the two marginal early pairs. This small slope adjustment aims to reach full resolution without consuming the later pair’s resolution margin or incurring a time penalty.

Use a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, between injections 7 and 8, to balance the marginal early and later pairs. The endpoint remains above the observed elution window, so this grid-valid method should preserve gradient elution while targeting full resolution.

Injection 9 achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping the endpoint and duration fixed to test a shorter fully resolved separation, with the shallower slope potentially offsetting early-pair compression.

Make the gradient shallower at the higher starting composition to recover resolution of the early critical pair. This tests whether injection 10 can become fully resolved while remaining faster than the maximum-score benchmark from injection 9.

The higher-starting-composition trials trade one critical pair against another at 60 C, while injection 9 already secures the maximum score. Test a substantially lower temperature with a moderately steep gradient to seek a different selectivity pattern that could support a faster fully resolved method.

Trim the low-organic portion of injection 12 while making the gradient shallower to test whether the remaining close pair separates. The first peak’s estimated elution composition was about 0.28, leaving retention margin at a starting fraction of 0.20 and potentially shortening the separation.

The close pair remained nearly unchanged after trimming the gradient window, suggesting temperature is the more useful selectivity lever. Raise temperature one step with the gradient fixed to seek full resolution and a shorter separation, retaining injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Hold temperature and endpoints fixed while lengthening the gradient to measure the remaining critical pair’s slope response directly. Injection 14 leaves enough time margin to test improved resolution without an expected time penalty; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

At 30 C, flattening the gradient improved one early gap but closed its neighbor; 25 C provided substantially more room in that neighboring gap. Combine 25 C with a shallower, trimmed gradient to seek full resolution while reducing time spent before the first peak.

Raise temperature one step from injection 16 to shift the persistent close pair while retaining its neighboring resolution margins. This also targets a last peak below the 7.45-minute maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the maximum-score region and test a slightly steeper slope than injection 9 to shorten the separation. This small grid-valid adjustment probes whether the early critical pairs retain full resolution while improving the later pair’s margin.

The faster slope at 60 C narrowly lost full resolution, and injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark. Test intermediate-temperature selectivity with a trimmed, shallower gradient to look for another fully resolved region with a shorter last-peak time.

Raise temperature to 60 C with injection 19’s gradient fixed to test whether its compact elution window can retain favorable high-temperature selectivity. Injection 9 remains the established maximum-score method while this trial seeks a faster alternative.

Test a substantially shallower gradient at the intermediate starting fraction to separate the early cluster and potentially move the later critical pair past its selectivity crossover. Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF; this trial seeks an alternative fully resolved method with greater resolution margins.

Injection 21 suggests the later critical pair has crossed elution order and is separating again as the gradient becomes shallower. Extend that trend while raising the starting organic fraction to offset retention time, seeking a second fully resolved method with larger resolution margins.

Refine around the maximum-score method from injection 9 by trimming the endpoint and shortening the programmed gradient, with a slightly shallower slope. This tests whether all peaks can remain fully resolved with a smaller solvent window; injection 9 remains the benchmark.

Return to injection 6’s lower starting fraction and slightly flatten its gradient to improve the early pair that narrowly missed full resolution. This tests a nearby balance of the competing critical pairs while preserving injection 9 as the established maximum-score method.

Use the final injection to extend the post-crossover separation suggested by injection 21, aiming for an alternative with stronger resolution margins despite a possible small time penalty. Injection 9 remains the campaign’s proven maximum-score method: CRF 1.000 with all eight peaks resolved by 7.45 minutes.
